extracted_claims.text: AI systems used in recruitment and selection (Annex III, point 4(a)), as well as promotion/task allocation/monitoring (4(b)) and emotional/behavioural monitoring of workers (4(c)), are classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act.

High-risk classification for employment AI under Annex III point 4 is categorical, with no materiality threshold or small-deployer carve-out, though Article 6(3) provides a narrow-risk derogation that does not apply where profiling of natural persons occurs.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must complete a conformity assessment (internal control under Annex VI for most Annex III categories), draw up an EU declaration of conformity, and affix CE marking before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.

Core obligations for high-risk AI systems include a risk management system (Art. 9), data and data governance (Art. 10), technical documentation (Art. 11), record-keeping (Art. 12), transparency/provision of information (Art. 13), human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity requirements.
Human oversight is described as the core deployer obligation for high-risk HR AI systems.

Deployers of recruitment chatbots or AI-driven screening tools (e.g., built on generative AI platforms) must provide Article 50 transparency disclosures to candidates before or at the start of the AI interaction.
Providers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III must register the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service.
Obligations for employment AI providers and deployers include risk assessments, technical documentation, bias testing, human oversight, transparency disclosures, and continuous monitoring.
Prohibited AI practices under Article 5 have already entered into force and are being enforced.

Transparency obligations (including Article 50) entered into application and became enforceable from 2 August 2026, with providers of systems placed on the market before that date given until 2 December 2026 to comply with Article 50(2) marking/detection obligations.
The AI Office and national authorities assumed general enforcement powers on 2 August 2026.
The original 2 August 2026 deadline for Annex III high-risk obligations (including employment/HR systems) was extended to 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus for AI agreement.
Some sources, prior to or around the Digital Omnibus agreement, state that Annex III high-risk enforcement (including HR/employment AI) begins/began 2 August 2026.
A further extension to 2 August 2030 applies to high-risk AI systems intended to be embedded in regulated products (Annex I), separate from the Annex III timeline.

Even though standalone high-risk (Annex III) obligations are deferred to 2 December 2027, foundational duties such as AI literacy under Article 4 and other preparatory obligations remain applicable now, and the deferral should not be treated as a reason to pause governance efforts.
Non-compliance with high-risk (Annex III) obligations can result in fines up to €15 million or 3% of global annual turnover.
Violations of prohibited AI practices (Article 5) can result in fines up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover.
Supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities can result in fines up to €7.5 million or 1% of global annual turnover.
GPAI providers face Commission enforcement, with fines up to €15 million or 3% of global annual turnover, effective from August 2026.

open_issues: No sources describe any specific, concrete enforcement actions, fines, or investigations that have actually been taken against companies for high-risk AI hiring tools to date; all enforcement information is about the penalty framework and dates of applicability, not actual cases.

It is unclear from the sources exactly which specific conformity assessment procedure (notified body involvement vs. internal control) applies to each employment sub-category (4(a), 4(b), 4(c)) given conflicting indications about points 2-8 of Annex III.

The sources do not clarify how the AI Pact's voluntary compliance commitments interact with the now-binding Digital Omnibus deadlines, i.e., whether early voluntary compliance confers any legal benefit.
It is unclear whether the EU database registration obligation (Article 71) is already enforceable now or also deferred to December 2027 along with other Annex III obligations.
The sources do not specify whether national authorities in EU member states have begun independent enforcement actions distinct from the AI Office at the EU level.
It is unclear how the Article 6(3) narrow-risk derogation would apply in practice to specific hiring tools beyond the general statement that it is unavailable where profiling occurs.
report:
# Compliance Requirements for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
AI hiring tools covering recruitment, selection, promotion, task allocation, monitoring, and emotional/behavioural analysis of workers are categorically classified as high-risk under Annex III of the EU AI Act (high confidence), triggering obligations around conformity assessment, risk management, data governance, documentation, and human oversight. While the AI Office and national authorities gained general enforcement powers on 2 August 2026 and transparency obligations are now enforceable, the core Annex III high-risk obligations for employment AI—originally due 2 August 2026—were extended to 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus agreement (high confidence). No sources report concrete enforcement actions, fines, or investigations yet taken against specific companies for hiring tools.

## Key Findings

### Classification and Scope
AI systems used in recruitment and selection (Annex III, point 4(a)), promotion/task allocation/monitoring (4(b)), and emotional/behavioural monitoring of workers (4(c)) are classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/employment-0), [Knowlee](https://www.knowlee.ai/blog/ai-act-annex-iii-hr-employment), [GLACIS](https://www.glacis.io/guide-employment-ai-high-risk). This classification is categorical with no materiality threshold or small-deployer carve-out, though a narrow Article 6(3) derogation exists that does not apply where profiling of natural persons occurs (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6), [Regulation AI](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/sectors/hr-recruitment).

### Core Compliance Obligations
Providers must complete a conformity assessment (generally internal control under Annex VI for most Annex III categories), issue an EU declaration of conformity, and affix CE marking before market placement (high confidence) [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf). Core obligations also include a risk management system, data and data governance measures, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency/information provision, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity requirements (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-71). Providers must register high-risk systems in the EU database before market placement (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-71). One lower-confidence source frames human oversight as the central deployer obligation specifically for HR AI [CheckCompliance.eu](https://www.checkcompliance.eu/eu-ai-act-hr-compliance), and the same source (low confidence) states deployers of recruitment chatbots must provide Article 50 transparency disclosures to candidates. Another medium-confidence source broadly lists risk assessments, bias testing, and continuous monitoring as employment AI obligations [EU AI Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/what-the-act-means-for-staffing-businesses).

### Timeline and Enforcement Status
Prohibited AI practices under Article 5 are already in force and being enforced (medium confidence) [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/04/us-companies-face-eu-ai-acts-possible-august-2026-compliance-deadline). Transparency obligations, including Article 50, became enforceable from 2 August 2026, with a further grace period to 2 December 2026 for marking/detection duties on pre-existing systems (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-enforcement-start). The AI Office and national authorities assumed general enforcement powers on 2 August 2026 (high confidence) [Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-pact). Critically, the original 2 August 2026 deadline for Annex III high-risk obligations—including employment/HR systems—was extended to 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus for AI agreement (high confidence) [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass), [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727). A separate extension to 2 August 2030 applies to high-risk systems embedded in regulated products under Annex I (medium confidence) [DLA Piper](https://intelligence.dlapiper.com/artificial-intelligence?t=08-enforcement&c=EU). Despite deferral of Annex III obligations, foundational duties such as AI literacy (Article 4) remain applicable now (medium confidence) [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass).

### Penalties
Non-compliance with Annex III obligations can theoretically result in fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover (low confidence) [GLACIS](https://www.glacis.io/guide-employment-ai-high-risk). Violations of prohibited practices could reach €35 million or 7% of turnover (low confidence) [Orbiq](https://www.orbiqhq.com/eu-regulations/eu-ai-act-compliance), while misleading authorities could incur fines up to €7.5 million or 1% of turnover (low confidence) [Orbiq](https://www.orbiqhq.com/eu-regulations/eu-ai-act-compliance).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Older or undated sources describe August 2026 as the operative Annex III deadline for HR/employment AI [Knowlee](https://www.knowlee.ai/blog/ai-act-annex-iii-hr-employment), while sources reflecting the Digital Omnibus agreement confirm extension to December 2027 [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass), rendering the earlier claims outdated. Several enforcement/penalty claims are low confidence (below 0.4), including human oversight framing, chatbot transparency duties, fine amounts for Annex III and Article 5 violations, and GPAI fines—these should be treated cautiously pending more authoritative confirmation.

## Knowledge Gaps
No sources document actual enforcement actions, fines, or investigations against companies for high-risk hiring tools. It remains unclear which conformity assessment procedure applies specifically to each employment sub-category, whether EU database registration is deferred alongside other Annex III duties, how AI Pact voluntary commitments interact with binding deadlines, whether member states are pursuing independent enforcement, and how the Article 6(3) derogation applies in practice to specific hiring tools.

2. [EU AI Act Annex III HR & Employment | Knowlee](https://www.knowlee.ai/blog/ai-act-annex-iii-hr-employment)
